title: Parents of Students With Disabilities Find Private School Vouchers Come With a Catch e-with-a-catch/
author: Pepper Stetler
summary: Pepper Stetler builds a reported case around Annabelle Kelly, a fifteen year old with Rett syndrome whose grandparents used Ohio's Jon Peterson scholarship to enroll her at a private Christian school, only to be told three months later that her needs were too extensive unless the family paid roughly $25,000 a year for an aide. The article's argument is legal rather than anecdotal: a student who takes a voucher becomes parentally placed, which means the private school owes her no IEP and none of the protections of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, including the protection against being removed because of a disability. Stetler shows that nothing in the Ohio program obliges anyone to tell parents they are surrendering those rights, and that the state's own guidance never says so plainly. She situates the case in the rapid growth of voucher use by students with disabilities, past 200,000 nationally, and in the failure of disability rights groups to get IDEA compliance written into the new federal program. The piece is careful to give the other side of the ledger through Nicole White, whose daughter thrived at a school for the deaf until budget cuts stripped her therapies away. The common thread is the absence of recourse: on paper Ohio asks private schools to employ credentialed staff and report IEP progress, but attaches no consequence when they do not.
points: Because voucher students are legally considered parentally placed, private schools owe them no IEP and no IDEA protections, including protection against removal on the basis of disability.

Neither Ohio's Jon Peterson scholarship nor the participating schools are required to tell families they are waiving those rights, and Ohio's education department website never states plainly that private schools need not comply with IDEA.

Congress declined to write an IDEA compliance requirement into last year's federal voucher legislation despite lobbying from disability rights groups, so advocates are now pressing individual states to impose one.

Stetler balances the reporting with the case of Kate White, whose family found real support at a school for the deaf until budget cuts eliminated her occupational and physical therapy and the family concluded she needed a more inclusive setting.
Ohio's rules look comparatively strict on paper, requiring credentialed staff, written denial reasons and IEP progress reporting, yet the state lists no consequences for schools that ignore them.
quotes: Disability advocates warn that as private school voucher programs spread, more parents will find themselves in similar straits. Federal protections for students with disabilities don’t apply to private schools, and neither the schools nor voucher programs like the one Annabelle qualified for are required to inform parents that they waive certain rights when they leave the public school system.

If there are public funds being spent, public protections need to be afforded,” said Chris Roe, director of state policy at the Council of Parent Attorneys and Advocates, a policy advocacy organization that provides training and guidance in special education law.

Students using a private school voucher are considered “parentally placed,” and private schools are not required to follow an IEP or uphold any IDEA protections. Families that use these vouchers sacrifice key civil rights afforded by the IDEA, including protection against discrimination and removal from the school based on a disability.

Kelly doesn’t remember, when filling out the scholarship application and enrolling Annabelle at CCS, being told that the rights and protections that apply to students with disabilities in public schools do not extend to private schools.

Schools receiving scholarship funds are also expected to provide the student’s assigned public school district with records of how the IEP was implemented and how the student is progressing toward its goals. But there are no consequences listed for schools that do not follow these rules.

Parents are enticed by the idea that they don’t have to fight their public school anymore for what they should be getting under the law,” he said. “But then they realize there are few schools that will take a child with nonverbal autism or with Down syndrome.
Private schools meant for students with disabilities can provide valuable support, he said, but students sacrifice an opportunity to learn among nondisabled peers.

But at the meeting in November, Kelly said, the school’s director of academic support services told her and Grimmer that Annabelle’s physical and educational needs were too extensive for her to continue at CCS.
